## What would full support look like?

For Day 8's Utopia theme, I wanted an environmental target with a measurable gap. Across Ohio's 1,538 watershed assessment units in this comparison, 513 fully support every reported aquatic-life use. Another 923 have at least one aquatic-life use marked “Not Supporting.” The remaining 102 have unassessed uses or insufficient information to establish full support. That puts 33.4% of the included units in the fully supporting group.

The map shows those reported results. The Utopian goal sits above it in one line: every watershed supports its aquatic-life uses. Robert Berry's Day 8 map of Welsh rivers, shared with me as a reference, prompted this approach. Ohio's reporting geography requires a different treatment: the colours belong to watershed units, with streams drawn over them for context.

## Method

EPA ATTAINS supplies the assessment decisions. I selected Ohio's organization `21OHIO` and the **2024 reporting cycle with EPA Final Action**. The 2026 report was available at the state-submittal stage when I retrieved the data; I used the completed 2024 cycle for this comparison.

Each unit can have several designated aquatic-life uses, including warmwater, coldwater, exceptional warmwater and modified habitats. A unit is green only when every reported aquatic-life use has code `F`, fully supporting. Any `N`, not supporting, puts the unit in the unmet group, even if another use supports its target or remains unassessed. Units without a known failure but with `I`, insufficient information, or `X`, not assessed, remain unresolved. The [use-level reduction](aquatic-uses.csv) preserves those distinctions.

The denominator is all 1,538 included watershed units, including the unresolved group. It is a count of units, not a percentage of river length, Ohio's land area, monitoring sites, or all water bodies. I excluded 55 river and seven Great Lakes open-water assessment units from the report because combining those with watershed polygons would mix reporting scales.

Every watershed record has an authoritative HUC12 identifier in ATTAINS. I joined that identifier to USGS watershed geometry, clipped the polygons to Ohio, and mapped the reported status in NAD83 / Conus Albers. Boundaries are simplified for display; the assessment counts come from identifiers, not polygon area.

## Data & provenance

Sources were retrieved November 11–12, 2026. [ATTAINS](https://www.epa.gov/waterdata/get-data-access-public-attains-data) records a reporting cycle, not simultaneous measurements of every stream in that year. The saved use records retain monitoring dates where reported. Some underlying observations are substantially older than 2024.

[Freshwater Explorer](https://www.epa.gov/water-research/freshwater-explorer) contributes named-stream geometry through its predicted-background-conductivity layer. The conductivity predictions are not used as measurements, impairment criteria, or evidence of aquatic-life attainment. The [watershed geometry](https://hydro.nationalmap.gov/arcgis/rest/services/wbd/MapServer) comes from USGS WBD; the state outline comes from [Census TIGERweb](https://tigerweb.geo.census.gov/arcgis/rest/services/TIGERweb/State_County/MapServer). These federal datasets are publicly available; source metadata and limitations still govern their interpretation.

The [acquisition script](acquire-data.R) is the explicit network step. ATTAINS credentials stay in an environment variable and HTTP header. A full named-reach ID inventory checks download completeness. The [source snapshot](source-snapshot.json) records query URLs and SHA-256 values. The [renderer](render-map.R) reads the committed [GeoPackage](ohio-map.gpkg) and [assessment table](assessments.csv) offline.

## What I learned

“Fully supporting” is use-specific. It does not mean pristine, safe to drink, safe to swim in, or free of every contaminant. Equally, a watershed result cannot classify each stream reach inside it. Keeping the reporting boundaries visible makes the aspiration more precise: every included unit supports all its reported aquatic-life uses, with the unresolved evidence gap acknowledged alongside the reported results.

**Alt text:** A single Ohio map of watershed assessment units coloured by reported aquatic-life support, with named streams shown as neutral geographic context and a short full-support goal above.
